analysis.file_name: The First Test Of The Texas Data Center Freeze Is Core Scientific's $1.3 Billion Building For AMD.pdf
analysis.title: The First Test Of The Texas Data Center Freeze Is Core Scientific's $1.3 Billion Building For AMD
key_insights: A Core Scientific (CORZ) subsidiary, Telios Quinlan One LLC, registered a $1.3B, 341,326 sq ft data center shell in Quinlan, Hunt County, Texas with the state licensing department (TDLR). Construction is listed to start Nov 24, 2026 and run to Sept 4, 2028. The filing names no tenant.

Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa is sworn in Jan 19, 2027, eight weeks after the listed construction start. She won on a pledge to freeze data center approvals until the Legislature writes new rules. The author calls this the first real-world test of the sellside assumption that projects already under construction are safe.

The author infers the filing is the AMD building. AMD signed 15-year leases in July for about 530 MW across five Core Scientific campuses, 110 MW of it in Hunt County. At management's $11-12M per MW build cost, $1.3B implies 108-118 MW. About 175 MW of leasable capacity on the campus remains to come (285 MW leasable of 430 MW gross).
The TDLR filing is an accessibility-standards plan review, not a power, water or siting approval. Registration does not mean a state agency has approved the data center.

Hinojosa's stated rule: 'It's for all permits.' She also said that if projects 'have already received state permits, I don't have the power just to shut them down.' The author reads this as: a project with every state permit proceeds, and one missing any permit waits for a Legislature that convenes Jan 12 and adjourns May 31. Wells Fargo's Revich describes the election as turning an audit-linked pause into a legislation-linked one.

Hunt County has most items secured. ERCOT approved the power in Oct 2024, $33M of cash collateral was posted to the co-op, the stormwater permit is held, the tenant is signed, and the equity for the first 530 MW of AMD capacity is funded from cash. Hunt was included in the November Quarterly Stability Assessment, which the CEO called the last milestone before energization.

The open item is the TCEQ air permits for backup diesel generators at Hunt and Pecos. TCEQ has been under orders since Sept 21 not to issue data center permits, and will report to the new governor. Management expects permit-by-rule treatment and could change the backup generator design. The CEO said 'things are never done retroactively' in Texas but did not address timing around the January handover.

Pecos behind-the-meter gas projects need air permits that management says have not been filed. The author argues campuses with their own power could have more paperwork at the frozen agency than grid-connected ones.

Sellside Texas risk estimates exclude under-construction assets. Morgan Stanley puts 8.3 GW of Texas capacity at risk through 2030, Bernstein applies a 30% Texas haircut while assuming 21 GW under construction is grandfathered, and Goldman's Ng shows Texas at 20% of 2027 and 27% of 2028 net additions on an under-construction basis.

Goldman's Ng notes moratoriums are not bans or cancellations, and the risks are ready-for-service delays (some leading to contract cancellations), higher financing costs, lost tax breaks and higher infrastructure capex. Ng also flagged that the tracker counts land clearing, grading and trenching as construction, so a moratorium could still catch a project lacking an air permit.

GLJ's Gordon Johnson triages projects in three buckets: power, permits and steel keep going, power without state environmental permits slips 12-18 months, and neither goes to Louisiana, Oklahoma or nowhere. The author places Core Scientific in the middle bucket. A 12-18 month slip would move a Sept 2028 completion into the back half of 2029.

Financing is a stress point. Core Scientific needs to sell project bonds against five AMD leases. Blackstone's QTS recently placed only $300M of an $800M deal, and Core Scientific's 7.75% 2031 notes fell 5 points to 92 after the Nov 3 vote.

Core Scientific is exiting bitcoin mining by year-end. Colocation was $215M of $233M Q3 revenue, CoreWeave is the anchor customer and AMD is the growth story. The stock was about $13.5 on Monday, down about 7%, and below half its $30.46 52-week high.

Moratorium risk is spreading beyond Texas. Arizona's AG, governor's office and incoming Senate president said a moratorium will be taken up in January. The Georgia, Ohio and Michigan governors-elect ran on pauses. Minneapolis capped new data centers at 50,000 sq ft of server space. Sanders called for a national moratorium, which the author says will not survive a veto. Of 45 data center votes on election day, one went the industry's way.

Goldman's Hatzius said Democratic state and local wins are likely to lead to short-term data center moratoria, potentially affecting about 45% of planned US data center capacity expansion. Texas is about a quarter of that planned capacity.

The author's view: the shell likely gets built, but the generator approval will be decided by a TCEQ answering to the new governor, on a legislative timetable. The author leans toward a slower and messier outcome than consensus. If TCEQ approves generators for projects with power, the 'under construction is safe' assumption holds. If 'all permits' means all, the next haircut falls on gigawatts treated as safe.

The author expects a rush of Texas groundbreakings before Jan 19, since every developer with a power agreement and tenant has the same window. Next checkpoints are the ERCOT audit due Dec 10 and whether steel is standing in Quinlan on inauguration day.

market_movers.rationale: Hunt County build is the first test of Texas moratorium treatment of under-construction projects. Pending TCEQ generator air permits and project bond financing could delay the AMD-leased building by 12-18 months.

sector_views.rationale: The author leans toward a slower and messier outcome than consensus, with permit-linked delays risking gigawatts the sellside treats as safe.

tension_points.bull_case: Projects with power, permits and steel keep going. Core Scientific's Hunt site has ERCOT power since Oct 2024, a signed AMD tenant, cash-funded equity and a stormwater permit. Hinojosa said she cannot shut down projects that already have state permits, and Morgan Stanley and Bernstein assume under-construction assets proceed.
tension_points.bear_case: Hinojosa said the moratorium is 'for all permits', and Hunt's backup generator air permits are still pending at TCEQ. GLJ's Johnson sees such projects slipping 12-18 months. Trackers count grading and trenching as construction, so Ng's 20% and 27% figures may include unprotected projects. Project bond financing is also strained.
tension_points.what_invalidates: TCEQ waving through backup generator permits for projects that already have power would confirm the 'under construction is safe' view. A TCEQ refusal or long delay after Jan 19 would break it.

theme_stances.key_argument: A governor who won promising a freeze is unlikely to open her term by carving out exceptions for AI landlords, so the outcome is slower and messier than consensus assumes.
theme_stances.evidence: We lean toward a slower and messier outcome than the consensus has penciled in
